response.text:
I would keep it as the voluntary game described here.

Someone can appreciate getting points for cleaning; someone else can clean without wanting a score. Neither preference needs to become the cooperative’s philosophy. The complaints about distraction remain real, but a member can now leave the game without losing income, membership or a turn at a workstation. That changes what the scoreboard allows anyone to demand of them.

The points still miss patient attention. They can nevertheless make some contributions visible. A game doesn’t have to contain a complete theory of human value to be worth playing. Trouble begins when its necessarily partial account acquires authority over everyone else.

Keep the existing categories and make withdrawal straightforward. Coordinators should describe the dashboard as an optional activity, and cooperative decisions should preserve the stipulated independence of pay, membership and access. Leave room for members to acknowledge help in ordinary conversation, without requiring either a score or a public performance of gratitude.

At the next regular review, hear briefly from participants and nonparticipants about how this arrangement works. There is no evidence here that informal pressure has defeated the right to leave, so I wouldn’t assume it has. If that changes, address the pressure. For now, letting people enjoy, ignore or abandon the game seems entirely reasonable.
